title: Rolling Hills Asylum, The New York Poorhouse That's Full Of Mysterious 'Shadow People'
excerpt: Rolling Hills Asylum in East Bethany, New York, originally opened as a working poor farm in 1827.
content:
The Chilling Story Of Rolling Hills Asylum And The ‘Shadow People’ That Haunt Its Halls

Published October 27, 2026

Rolling Hills Asylum opened in Upstate New York as a poorhouse in 1827, and today visitors to the allegedly haunted site report floating orbs, disembodied voices, and the shadowy spirits of former residents.

Genesee County Chamber of CommerceRolling Hills Asylum, the former Genesee County Poor Farm that’s said to be haunted by the ghosts of its former residents.

Today, Rolling Hills Asylum is a paranormal tourist attraction in Upstate New York. But its story began 200 years ago, when the facility was still known as the Genesee County Poor Farm.

The institution opened in 1827, and over the decades it served as a poorhouse, infirmary, tuberculosis clinic, orphanage, and nursing home. It closed in 1974 — and since then, countless stories have emerged about the spirits that purportedly haunt its halls.

Its most infamous ghosts are the “Shadow People” that are often spotted in dim corridors throughout the building. There are also tales of former residents, disembodied voices, and even cruel nurses who still maintain a sinister presence within the facility’s walls.

Take a look inside Rolling Hills Asylum — and decide for yourself whether it’s truly as haunted as it’s said to be.

The Origins Of The Genesee County Poor Farm

In December 1826, the Batavia Times reported that a new poorhouse would be opening in East Bethany, New York — roughly halfway between Rochester and Buffalo. According to the Genesee County government, the institution would be “ready for the reception of paupers on the first day of 1827.”

The facility was meant for vagrants, drunkards, “lunatics,” paupers, and other citizens who struggled to maintain housing. By the 1860s, there were more than 1,000 residents — and 700 of them were there due to excessive alcohol consumption. Others had physical or mental health issues, and some simply struggled to support themselves after the death of a family member and subsequent loss of wages.

Genesee County History DepartmentA historical photo of Rolling Hills Asylum from its time as a working poor farm.

The institution eventually operated as a self-sustaining working farm. Residents who were able to help were assigned specific tasks, from growing, harvesting, and canning food to taking care of livestock and chopping down trees to use for heating. There was also an on-site bakery and a wood workshop where coffins were made.

Over the decades, a wide variety of residents entered the poorhouse. Orphans, tuberculosis patients, the sick, and the elderly all called the property home. It remained in operation under various capacities for nearly 150 years, ultimately closing its doors in 1974.

The building then sat abandoned for years before ultimately reopening as a paranormal attraction called Rolling Hills Asylum.

A New Life For The Historic Poorhouse

When Sharon Coyle purchased the former Genesee County Poor Farm in 2009, her main goal was to preserve the historic property. Of course, she was also fascinated by the paranormal rumors that surrounded the 60,000-square-foot facility.

“When I learned that RHA was closing forever, I had to intervene” Coyle told the Genesee Valley Penny Saver in 2022.

Genesee County GovernmentThe eerie hallways at Rolling Hills Asylum are allegedly rife with paranormal activity.

She eventually opened the building for guided tours and ghost hunts, and today it’s a popular tourist attraction in Upstate New York. “It gives people who have lost a loved one hope that there is something afterwards,” Coyle said. “[Visitors] come from all over: Alaska, Texas, England, Australia, and more.”

As it became clear that people were just as fascinated by the paranormal as Coyle was, Rolling Hills Asylum began offering even more experiences for guests. There are seminars, special events, and even classes that teach hopeful ghost hunters how to operate the various cameras, recording devices, and meters used by professional paranormal investigators.

Thousands of people visit Rolling Hills Asylum each year — and many of them leave with chilling stories to tell.

Over the years, visitors have reported countless paranormal experiences at Rolling Hills Asylum. In the building’s East Wing, people sometimes hear a voice calling out “Hello!” from a room where a woman named Hattie once lived. Hattie was blind, and she purportedly shouted “Hello!” at her nurses to get their attention.

Julie Buckner/Rolling Hills AsylumRolling Hills Asylum volunteer Julie Buckner captured this photo of what appears to be a ghostly face peering through a window.

Guests also hear ghostly voices from the morgue — and when they enter, they sometimes feel as if they’re being shoved. Then, there’s the voice of Nurse Emmie. She was supposedly known for her cruelty, and she allegedly held Satanic rituals within the institution and used black magic on her patients. Visitors report hearing her sinister cackle from the infirmary.

But perhaps the most infamous spirits at the asylum are the Shadow People. These dark figures are often seen in the hallways. They usually keep their distance and vanish quickly, but they’ve also been known to creepily crawl straight toward visitors.

Renowned psychic medium Chris Fleming visited Rolling Hills Asylum in 2008 and witnessed these Shadow People for himself. According to the asylum’s official website, Fleming recalled: “The moonlight was shining through the large window and there was a solid male figure standing in front of the illuminated sill staring right at us.” The shadowy man then “imploded into a small black mist of shadow.”

Rolling Hills Asylum/FacebookA purported Shadow Person in the “Shadow Hallway” in the former men’s dormitory at Rolling Hills Asylum.

As the owner of the building, Coyle has the eeriest stories of all. As she told the Penny Saver, “There are so many things we see, feel, hear, and smell. Things moving right in front of us… We will witness clocks chiming, whistling, a wheelchair rolling on its own, words coming through a spirit box, all kinds of things.”

“Guests have experienced little children’s hands grabbing onto their hands,” Coyle continued, “hearing their names called out, sitting in the barber’s chair and feeling hair falling on their face like they were having a haircut… It’s crazy, amazing, and phenomenal.”

Her favorite spirit is Roy Crouse, a former resident who suffered from gigantism. He grew to be seven feet tall, and his towering figure is one of the most commonly seen Shadow People at the asylum.

Shortly after Coyle purchased the property, she was startled by a rat in the infirmary. The next day, she found it dead on the stairs — and she believes that Crouse killed it for her. Ever since then, Coyle says, Crouse will sometimes “call out my name in his deep voice.”

Jaimiemgrant/TripadvisorAn abandoned nursery at the former Genesee County Poor Farm.

“We also have a little boy named Jacque,” Coyle told the Penny Saver. “He looks like Pugsley from The Addams Family.” She was once putting something away in the laundry room when Jacque’s spirit allegedly shouted, “Boo!”

“I scolded him for startling me,” Coyle said. “A year later, I asked him if he wanted to say boo to me through the spirit box, and he did. That is his little signal to me.”

Together, all of these incidents — from Jacque’s small “boo” to the countless sightings of Shadow People — seemingly make Rolling Hills Asylum one of the most haunted spots in Upstate New York. Of course, the only way to find out for certain if the stories are true is to pay a visit yourself.
